{{Short description|Things associated with unlawful behavior}}
{{Criminology}}
The '''correlates of crime''' explore the associations of specific non-criminal factors with specific crimes.

The field of [[criminology]] studies the dynamics of crime. Most of these studies use [[Correlation (statistics)|correlational]] data; that is, they attempt to identify various factors are associated with specific categories of criminal behavior. Such correlational studies led to hypotheses about the causes of these crimes.

''The Handbook of Crime Correlates'' (2009) is a systematic review of 5200 empirical studies on crime that have been published worldwide. A crime consistency score represents the strength of relationships. The scoring depends on how consistently a [[statistically significant]] relationship was identified across multiple studies. The authors claim that the review summarizes most of what is currently known about the variables associated with criminality.{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}} Writing in 2019, criminologist Greg Ridgeway argued that criminology was still trying to conclusively determine what causes crime.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1146/annurev-statistics-030718-105057|title=Experiments in Criminology: Improving Our Understanding of Crime and the Criminal Justice System|year=2019|last1=Ridgeway|first1=Greg|journal=[[Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application]]|volume=6|pages=37–61|s2cid=158290235 }}</ref>

Crime occurs most frequently during the second and third decades of life.{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}} 

==Sex==
{{Main|Sex differences in crime}}
Males commit more crime overall and more violent crime than females. They commit more property crime except [[shoplifting]], which is about equally distributed between the genders. Males appear to be more likely to [[Recidivism|reoffend]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Gender differences in life-course theory of recidivism: a survival analysis |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15851511/ |website=pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov |access-date=18 March 2026}}</ref>

==Genetics==
{{Main|Genetics and crime}}
{{anchor|Genetics}}
=== Serotonin ===
Lower [[serotonin|serotonergic]] activity in the brain is associated with criminality. Serotonin levels can be estimated by measuring the levels of the metabolite [[5-HIAA]] in the urine; offenders often have lower levels of 5-HIAA. An [[5-HTTLPR]] [[Gene polymorphism|polymorphism]], which lowers serotonin levels, has been found to be associated with criminal behavior. In addition, a lower density of [[paroxetine]] [[binding site]]s, which is associated with lower levels of serotonin transmission in the brain, is associated with greater criminality. {{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}}

=== Other ===
In addition, [[CDH13]], a gene previously tied to an increased risk of [[substance abuse]], has been tied to violent crime.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tiihonen |first1=J |last2=Rautiainen |first2=M-R |last3=Ollila |first3=H M |last4=Repo-Tiihonen |first4=E |last5=Virkkunen |first5=M |last6=Palotie |first6=A |last7=Pietiläinen |first7=O |last8=Kristiansson |first8=K |last9=Joukamaa |first9=M |last10=Lauerma |first10=H |last11=Saarela |first11=J |last12=Tyni |first12=S |last13=Vartiainen |first13=H |last14=Paananen |first14=J |last15=Goldman |first15=D |last16=Paunio |first16=T |title=Genetic background of extreme violent behavior |journal=Molecular Psychiatry |date=June 2015 |volume=20 |issue=6 |pages=786–792 |doi=10.1038/mp.2014.130 |pmid=25349169 |pmc=4776744 }}</ref> Low [[cholesterol]] levels, slow [[heart rate]], [[DHEA]], [[MHPG]], [[blood glucose]], [[cortisol]], [[testosterone]], and blood [[lead]] levels, and the ratio of [[tryptophan]] to other [[amino acid]]s in the blood, have all also been connected to criminal behavior. [[Physical attractiveness]] has been found to be negatively correlated with criminality.{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}} These tendencies are ostensibly related, as the majority of all individuals who commit severe violent crime [[Crime in Finland|in Finland]] do so under the influence of alcohol or drugs. The presence of the genetic profile is not determinative, although it increases the likelihood of [[wiktionary:Delinquency|delinquency]] in cases where other factors are present. Ferguson stated, 'a large percentage of our behaviour in terms of violence or aggression is influenced by our biology - our genes - and our brain anatomy.'<ref name=bbc>{{cite news |last1=Hogenboom |first1=Melissa |title=Two genes linked with violent crime |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-29760212 |work=BBC News |date=28 October 2014 }}</ref> Schnupp stated, 'To call these alleles "genes for violence" would therefore be a massive exaggeration. In combination with many other factors these genes may make it a little harder for you to control violent urges, but they most emphatically do not predetermine you for a life of crime.'<ref name=bbc/>

==Race, ethnicity ==
{{excerpt|Race and crime|paragraphs=1|only=paragraphs}}
In some countries, ethnically/racially diverse geographical areas have higher crime rates compared to homogeneous areas, and in other countries, it is the other way around.{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}} 

==Immigration status==
{{Main|Immigration and crime}}
While some studies on [[immigrants]] found higher rates of crime, this varies with the country of origin. Immigrants from some regions show lower reported crime rates than the native-born population.{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}} Notions about the propensity for immigrants to commit crime vary among geographical regions. Likewise, the propensity for immigrants to commit more or less crime than the native-born population also varies geographically. For instance within the United States, census data shows that immigrants are less likely to be incarcerated for a crime than residents who were born within the United States.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/immigrants-commit-crimes-us-united-states-born-america-donald-trump-alien-weekly-list-a7548956.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220524/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/immigrants-commit-crimes-us-united-states-born-america-donald-trump-alien-weekly-list-a7548956.html |archive-date=2022-05-24 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Immigrants less likely to commit crimes than those born in the US|date=2017-01-27|work=The Independent|access-date=2017-03-06|language=en-GB}}</ref> The United States census includes both legal and illegal immigrants, as it counts the total number of people residing in an area regardless of citizenship status.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/population/apportionment/about/faq.html|title=Congressional Apportionment - Frequently Asked Questions|access-date=November 13, 2019}}</ref>

==Early life==
Associated factors include [[Smoking and pregnancy|maternal smoking during pregnancy]], [[low birth weight]], [[perinatal]] trauma/birth complications,{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}}<ref name="Monea2011">{{cite journal |last1=Monea |first1=Emily |last2=Thomas |first2=Adam |title=Unintended Pregnancy and Taxpayer Spending |journal=Perspectives on Sexual and Reproductive Health |date=June 2011 |volume=43 |issue=2 |pages=88–93 |doi=10.1363/4308811 |pmid=21651707 }}</ref> [[child abuse|child maltreatment]], low parent-child attachment, marital discord/family discord, [[alcoholism]] and drug use in the family, low parental supervision/monitoring, family size and birth order,{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}} [[nocturnal enuresis]] or bed wetting, [[bullying]], school disciplinary problems, [[truancy]], low [[grade point average]], dropping out of high school{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}} and childhood lead exposure.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.motherjones.com/environment/2013/01/lead-crime-link-gasoline?page=1|title=Sick Kids Are Just the Beginning of America's Lead Crisis|work=Mother Jones|access-date=2017-03-06|language=en}}</ref>

==Adult behavior==
Associated factors include high alcohol use, alcohol abuse and alcoholism, high illegal drug use and dependence, [[Virginity#Early loss of virginity|early age of first sexual intercourse]] and the number of sexual partners, social isolation, criminal peer groups and gang membership.{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}}

==Religiosity==
{{See also|Religious violence}}
A few studies have found a negative correlation between [[religiosity]] and criminality. A 2001 [[meta-analysis]] found, "religious beliefs and behaviors exert a moderate deterrent effect on individuals' criminal behavior", but that "studies have systematically varied in their estimation of the religion-on-crime effect due to differences in both their conceptual and methodological approaches". This suggests that religiosity has been [[Operationalization|operationalized]] in varying ways, impacting the results of the findings.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baier |first1=Colin J. |last2=Wright |first2=Bradley R. E. |title='If You Love Me, Keep My Commandments': A Meta-Analysis of the Effect of Religion on Crime |journal=Journal of Research in Crime and Delinquency |date=February 2001 |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=3–21 |doi=10.1177/0022427801038001001 |s2cid=145779667 }}</ref> Additionally, 1995 paper stated that "[a]lthough a few researchers have found that religion's influence is noncontingent, most have found support—especially among youths—for effects that vary by denomination, type of offense, and social and/or religious context," suggesting a complex relationship between religiosity and crime. They also "found that, among our religiosity measures, participation in religious activities was a persistent and noncontingent inhibiter of adult crime" when controlling for other factors, such as social ecology and secular constraints.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Evans |first1=T. David |last2=Cullen |first2=Francis T. |last3=Dunaway |first3=R. Gregory |last4=Burton |first4=Velmer S. |title=Religion and Crime Reexamined: The Impact of Religion, Secular Controls, and Social Ecology on Adult Criminality |journal=Criminology |date=May 1995 |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=195–224 |doi=10.1111/j.1745-9125.1995.tb01176.x }}</ref>

An individual with high religious saliency (i.e. expressing the high importance of religion in their life) is less likely to be associated with criminal activities; similarly, an individual who regularly attends religious services or is highly involved in them tends to be less involved in criminality, with the exception of property damage.{{Sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}}{{rp|108}} Other meta-analysis research suggests that those who subscribe to more orthodox religious beliefs are less likely to engage in criminal behavior than those who do not.{{Sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}}{{rp|112}} A 2012 study suggested that belief in hell decreases crime rates, while belief in heaven increases them, and indicated that these correlations were stronger than other correlates like national wealth or income inequality.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shariff |first1=Azim F. |last2=Rhemtulla |first2=Mijke |title=Divergent Effects of Beliefs in Heaven and Hell on National Crime Rates |journal=PLOS ONE |date=18 June 2012 |volume=7 |issue=6 |article-number=e39048 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0039048 |pmid=22723927 |pmc=3377603 |bibcode=2012PLoSO...739048S |doi-access=free }}</ref>

A 1997 study of six public high schools found no statistically significant negative correlations between religiosity and crime, or religiosity and drug use, and the only relationship between religiosity and alcohol was statistically significant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Benda |first1=Brent B. |title=An Examination of a Reciprocal Relationship Between Religiosity and Different Forms of Delinquency Within a Theoretical Model |journal=Journal of Research in Crime and Delinquency |date=May 1997 |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=163–186 |doi=10.1177/0022427897034002001 |s2cid=146674490 }}</ref>  A more recent review concludes that there are insufficient data to indicate any correlation between religiosity and crime.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zuckerman |first1=Phil |title=Atheism, Secularity, and Well-Being: How the Findings of Social Science Counter Negative Stereotypes and Assumptions |journal=Sociology Compass |date=December 2009 |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=949–971 |doi=10.1111/j.1751-9020.2009.00247.x }}</ref> Furthermore, any possible correlations may not apply universally to all relatively nonreligious groups, as there is some evidence self-identified atheists have had significantly lower incarceration rates than the general public in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.adherents.com/misc/adh_prison.html#altformat|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001212040800/http://www.adherents.com/misc/adh_prison.html#altformat|url-status=usurped|archive-date=December 12, 2000|title=Prison Incarceration and Religious Preference}}</ref> Most studies examining correlation to date do not distinguish between different types of low religiosity.

==Political ideology==
A 2016 study found statistically significant evidence that [[political ideology]] is moderately correlated with involvement in non-violent crime, among white individuals and particularly among white women. It suggests that liberal self-classification can, among some groups, be positively associated with non-violent criminal behavior compared to conservative self-classification.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wright |first1=John Paul |last2=Beaver |first2=Kevin M. |last3=Morgan |first3=Mark Alden |last4=Connolly |first4=Eric J. |title=Political ideology predicts involvement in crime |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=February 2017 |volume=106 |pages=236–241 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2016.10.062 }}</ref>

==Psychological traits==
Associated factors include childhood [[conduct disorder]], adult [[antisocial personality disorder]] (also associated with each other),{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}}<ref name="WilsonPetersilia2002">{{cite book |first1=James Q.|last1= Wilson|first2=Joan |author-link1=James Q. Wilson|last2=Petersilia|title=Crime: public policies for crime control|url={{google books |plainurl=y |id=DJfaAAAAMAAJ}}|year=2002|publisher=ICS Press|isbn=978-1-55815-509-1}}</ref> [[attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]] (ADHD), minor [[Depression (mood)|depression]], clinical depression, depression in the family, suicidal tendencies and [[schizophrenia]].{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fazel |first1=Seena |last2=Grann |first2=Martin |title=The Population Impact of Severe Mental Illness on Violent Crime |journal=American Journal of Psychiatry |date=August 2006 |volume=163 |issue=8 |pages=1397–1403 |doi=10.1176/ajp.2006.163.8.1397 |pmid=16877653 |s2cid=23042885 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The [[American Psychological Association]]'s 1995 report ''Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns'' stated that the correlation between [[intelligence quotient]] (IQ) and crime was -0.2. This association is generally regarded as small and prone to disappear or be substantially reduced after controlling for the proper covariates, being much smaller than typical sociological correlates.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cullen |first1=Francis T. |last2=Gendreau |first2=Paul |last3=Jarjoura |first3=G. Roger |last4=Wright |first4=John Paul |title=Crime and the Bell Curve: Lessons from Intelligent Criminology |journal=Crime & Delinquency |date=October 1997 |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=387–411 |doi=10.1177/0011128797043004001 |s2cid=145418972 }}</ref> In his book ''[[The g Factor: The Science of Mental Ability]]'' (1998), Arthur Jensen cited data which showed that IQ was generally negatively associated with crime among people of all races, peaking between 80 and 90.  Learning disability is a substantial discrepancy between IQ and academic performance and is associated with crime. Slow reading development may be particularly relevant.{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}} It has also been shown, however, that the effect of IQ is heavily dependent on socioeconomic status and that it cannot be easily controlled away, with many methodological considerations being at play.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mears |first1=Daniel P. |last2=Cochran |first2=Joshua C. |title=What is the effect of IQ on offending? |journal=Criminal Justice and Behavior |date=November 2013 |volume=40 |issue=11 |pages=1280–1300 |doi=10.1177/0093854813485736 |s2cid=147219554 }}</ref> Indeed, there is evidence that the small relationship is mediated by well-being, substance abuse, and other confounding factors that prohibit simple causal interpretation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Freeman |first1=James |title=The relationship between lower intelligence, crime and custodial outcomes: a brief literary review of a vulnerable group |journal=Vulnerable Groups & Inclusion |date=January 2012 |volume=3 |issue=1 |article-number=14834 |doi=10.3402/vgi.v3i0.14834 |s2cid=145305072 |doi-access=free }}</ref> A recent meta-analysis has shown that the relationship is only observed in higher risk populations such as those in poverty without direct effect, but without any causal interpretation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ttofi |first1=Maria M. |last2=Farrington |first2=David P. |last3=Piquero |first3=Alex R. |last4=Lösel |first4=Friedrich |last5=DeLisi |first5=Matthew |last6=Murray |first6=Joseph |title=Intelligence as a protective factor against offending: A meta-analytic review of prospective longitudinal studies |journal=Journal of Criminal Justice |date=1 June 2016 |volume=45 |pages=4–18 |doi=10.1016/j.jcrimjus.2016.02.003 }}</ref> A nationally representative longitudinal study has shown that this relationship is entirely mediated by school performance.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=McGloin |first1=Jean Marie |last2=Pratt |first2=Travis C. |last3=Maahs |first3=Jeff |title=Rethinking the IQ-delinquency relationship: A longitudinal analysis of multiple theoretical models |journal=Justice Quarterly |date=1 September 2004 |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=603–635 |doi=10.1080/07418820400095921 |s2cid=143305924 }}</ref>

Several personality traits are associated with criminality: [[impulsivity]], [[psychoticism]], [[sensation-seeking]], low [[self control]], childhood [[aggression]], low [[empathy]] and low [[altruism]].{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}}

==Socioeconomic factors==
[[Socioeconomic status]] (usually measured using the three variables income or wealth, occupational level, and years of education) correlates negatively with criminality, except for self-reported illegal drug use. Higher parental socioeconomic status probably has an inverse relationship with crime. Unstable employment and high frequency of unemployment correlate positively with criminality.{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}}<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.knowswhy.com/why-do-celebrities-get-away-with-crimes/|title=Why do Celebrities get away with Crimes?|last=Morgan|date=22 May 2010|website=www.knowswhy.com|language=en-US|access-date=2017-03-06}}</ref> Low socioeconomic status is thought to be positively correlated with higher levels of stress, and therefore the mental and psychological ill-effects of stress.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baum |first1=Andrew |last2=Garofalo |first2=J. P. |last3=Yali |first3=Ann Marie |title=Socioeconomic Status and Chronic Stress: Does Stress Account for SES Effects on Health? |journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences |date=December 1999 |volume=896 |issue=1 |pages=131–144 |doi=10.1111/j.1749-6632.1999.tb08111.x |pmid=10681894 |bibcode=1999NYASA.896..131B |s2cid=41519491 }}</ref> Indeed, higher stress levels have been positively associated with a propensity to commit crime.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Felson |first=Richard B. |last2=Osgood |first2=D. Wayne |last3=Horney |first3=Julie |last4=Wiernik |first4=Craig |date=2012-06-01 |title=Having a Bad Month: General Versus Specific Effects of Stress on Crime |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10940-011-9138-6 |journal=Journal of Quantitative Criminology |language=en |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=347–363 |doi=10.1007/s10940-011-9138-6 |issn=1573-7799|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Somewhat inconsistent evidence indicates a positive relationship between low income levels, the percentage of population under the poverty line, low education levels, and high [[income inequality]] in an area with more crime in said area.{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}} A 2013 study from Sweden argued that there was little effect of neighbourhood deprivation on criminality per se and rather that the higher rates of crime were due to observed and unobserved family and individual level factors, indicating that high-risk individuals were being selected into economically deprived areas.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sariaslan |first1=Amir |last2=Långström |first2=Niklas |last3=D'Onofrio |first3=Brian |last4=Hallqvist |first4=Johan |last5=Franck |first5=Johan |last6=Lichtenstein |first6=Paul |title=The impact of neighbourhood deprivation on adolescent violent criminality and substance misuse: A longitudinal, quasi-experimental study of the total Swedish population |journal=International Journal of Epidemiology |date=1 August 2013 |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=1057–1066 |doi=10.1093/ije/dyt066 |pmid=24062294 |pmc=3780994 }}</ref>

A [[World Bank]] study said, "Crime rates and inequality are positively correlated within countries and, particularly, between countries, and this correlation reflects causation from inequality to crime rates, even after controlling for other crime determinants."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fajnzylber |first1=Pablo |last2=Lederman |first2=Daniel |last3=Loayza |first3=Norman |title=Inequality and Violent Crime |journal=The Journal of Law and Economics |date=April 2002 |volume=45 |issue=1 |pages=1–39 |doi=10.1086/338347 |citeseerx=10.1.1.559.483 |s2cid=11378886 }}</ref>

Researchers in criminology have argued the effect of poverty upon crime is contextual:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Brookman |first1=Fiona |last2=Robinson |first2=Amanda |chapter=Violent Crime |pages=563–594 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gI2pZWuVu28C&pg=PA563 |editor1-last=Morgan |editor1-first=Rod |editor2-last=Maguire |editor2-first=Mike |editor3-last=Reiner |editor3-first=Robert |title=The Oxford Handbook of Criminology |date=12 April 2012 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-959027-8 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wright |first1=Bradley R. Entner |last2=Caspi |first2=Avshalom |last3=Moffitt |first3=Terrie E. |last4=Miech |first4=Richard A. |last5=Silva |first5=Phil A. |title=Reconsidering the relationship between SES and delinquency: Causation but not correlation |journal=Criminology |date=February 1999 |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=175–194 |doi=10.1111/j.1745-9125.1999.tb00483.x }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | pmid=25147371 | date=2014 | last1=Sariaslan | first1=A. | last2=Larsson | first2=H. | last3=d'Onofrio | first3=B. | last4=Långström | first4=N. | last5=Lichtenstein | first5=P. | title=Childhood family income, adolescent violent criminality and substance misuse: Quasi-experimental total population study | journal=The British Journal of Psychiatry: The Journal of Mental Science | volume=205 | issue=4 | pages=286–290 | doi=10.1192/bjp.bp.113.136200 | pmc=4180846 }}</ref>

<blockquote>As Levi (1997: 860) noted, macrolevel accounts 'seldom generate anything close to a causal account which makes sense of nonviolence as well as of violence'. Put another way, the vast majority of individuals who live in conditions of poverty or disadvantage do not resort to violence at any time. Hence, in order to understand the patterns of violence that actually occur, it is imperative to study the social experiences of those who engage in it (Athens 1992).</blockquote>

==Geographic factors==
Associated factors include areas with population size, neighborhood quality, residential mobility, tavern and alcohol density, gambling and tourist density, proximity to the equator,{{sfn|Ellis|Beaver|Wright|2009}} temperature ([[weather]] and season). The higher crime rate in the southern US largely disappears after controlling for non-climatic factors.<ref name="Miller2009">{{cite book |first=J. Mitchell |last=Miller|title=21st Century Criminology: A Reference Handbook|url={{google books |plainurl=y |id=mDluKVUcJ8AC|page=412}}|date=18 August 2009|publisher=Sage|isbn=978-1-4129-6019-9|page=57}}</ref>

== Parent–child relationships ==
Children whose parents did not want children are more likely to commit crimes. Such children are less likely to succeed in school, and are more likely to live in poverty.<ref name="Monea2011" />  They tend to have lower mother{{nbnd}}child relationship quality.<ref name="HP2020FP">{{cite web | title = Family Planning – Healthy People 2020 | url = http://healthypeople.gov/2020/topicsobjectives2020/overview.aspx?topicid=13 | access-date = 2011-08-18 | archive-date = 2010-12-28 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20101228012908/http://www.healthypeople.gov/2020/topicsobjectives2020/overview.aspx?topicid=13 }}
Which cites:
* {{cite report |last1=Logan |first1=Cassandra |last2=Holcombe |first2=Emily |last3=Manlove |first3=Jennifer |last4=Ryan |first4=Suzanne |title=The Consequences of Unintended Childbearing |date=May 2007 |publisher=Child Trends |s2cid=4682087 |citeseerx=10.1.1.365.2689 }}
* {{cite journal |last1=Cheng |first1=Diana |last2=Schwarz |first2=Eleanor B. |last3=Douglas |first3=Erika |last4=Horon |first4=Isabelle |title=Unintended pregnancy and associated maternal preconception, prenatal and postpartum behaviors |journal=Contraception |date=March 2009 |volume=79 |issue=3 |pages=194–198 |doi=10.1016/j.contraception.2008.09.009 |pmid=19185672 }}
* {{cite journal |last1=Kost |first1=Kathryn |last2=Landry |first2=David J. |last3=Darroch |first3=Jacqueline E. |title=Predicting Maternal Behaviors During Pregnancy: Does Intention Status Matter? |journal=Family Planning Perspectives |date=March 1998 |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=79–88 |doi=10.2307/2991664 |pmid=9561873 |jstor=2991664 }}
* {{cite journal |last1=D'Angelo |first1=Denise V. |last2=Gilbert |first2=Brenda Colley |last3=Rochat |first3=Roger W. |last4=Santelli |first4=John S. |last5=Herold |first5=Joan M. |title=Differences Between Mistimed and Unwanted Pregnancies Among Women Who Have Live Births |journal=Perspectives on Sexual and Reproductive Health |date=2004 |volume=36 |issue=5 |pages=192–197 |doi=10.1363/3619204 |pmid=15519961 }}</ref>

==Biosocial criminology and other analysis of environmental factors==
{{main|Biosocial criminology|Environmental criminology}}
[[Biosocial criminology]] is an [[interdisciplinary]] field that aims to explain crime and antisocial behavior by exploring both biological factors and environmental factors. While contemporary criminology has been dominated by [[sociological]] theories, biosocial criminology also recognizes the potential contributions of fields such as [[genetics]], [[neuropsychology]] and [[evolutionary psychology]].<ref name=Asghate2011>{{cite book|first1=Anthony |last1=Walsh|first2=Kevin M |last2=Beaver|chapter=Biosocial Criminology|title=The Ashgate Research Companion to Biosocial Theories of Crime|chapter-url={{google books |plainurl=y |id=V9KhAgAAQBAJ}}|date=28 January 2013|publisher=Ashgate Publishing, Ltd.|isbn=978-1-4094-9470-6}}</ref>

Aggressive behavior has been associated with abnormalities in three principal regulatory systems in the body: 
* [[serotonin|serotonin systems]], 
* [[catecholamine|catecholamine systems]], 
* and the [[hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical axis]]. 
Abnormalities in these systems also are known to be induced by [[Stress (biology)|stress]], either severe, acute stress or chronic low-grade stress.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Walton |first1=Kenneth G. |last2=Levitsky |first2=Debra K. |title=Effects of the Transcendental Meditation Program on Neuroendocrine Abnormalities Associated with Aggression and Crime |journal=Journal of Offender Rehabilitation |date=11 August 2003 |volume=36 |issue=1–4 |pages=67–87 |doi=10.1300/J076v36n01_04 |s2cid=144374302 }}</ref>

In environmental terms, the [[Lead and crime hypothesis|theory that crime rates and lead exposure]] are connected, with increases in the latter causing increases in the former, has attracted much scientific analysis. In 2011, a report published by the official United Nations News Centre remarked, "Ridding the world of leaded petrol, with the United Nations leading the effort in developing countries, has resulted in $2.4 trillion in annual benefits, 1.2 million fewer premature deaths, higher overall intelligence and 58 million fewer crimes". The [[California State University]] did the specific study. Then [[United Nations Environment Programme|U.N. Environment Programme]] (UNEP) executive director [[Achim Steiner]] argued, "Although this global effort has often flown below the radar of media and global leaders, it is clear that the elimination of leaded petrol is an immense achievement on par with the global elimination of major deadly diseases."<ref name=UN>{{cite web |url=https://news.un.org/en/story/2011/10/393292-phase-out-leaded-petrol-brings-huge-health-and-cost-benefits-un-backed-study |title=Phase-out of leaded petrol brings huge health and cost benefits – UN–backed study |date=27 October 2011 |publisher=United Nations News Centre }}</ref>
